result.summary: Æneas tells Dido how the Greeks feigned departure and left a wooden horse, how Sinon's lies and Laocoon's death persuaded the Trojans to drag it in, and how Troy fell by night. After Priam's death, Venus stops Æneas from killing Helen and shows him the gods destroying Troy. He leads his family out, loses Creusa, and withdraws to the mountains with a band of exiles.

scenes.title: Æneas begins his tale
scenes.summary: At Dido's request Æneas reluctantly agrees to recount Troy's last agony.

scenes.title: The wooden horse
scenes.summary: The Greeks build a horse, hide in it and retreat to Tenedos. The Trojans debate, and Laocoon hurls a spear at it, warning against Greek gifts.
scenes.stakes: Troy's survival depends on whether the horse is admitted.

scenes.title: Sinon's deceit
scenes.summary: Shepherds bring in the captive Sinon, who tells a false tale of persecution by Ulysses and of the Palladium. Priam spares him and the Trojans believe the horse is sacred.
scenes.stakes: Sinon risks death; the Trojans risk being deceived.

scenes.title: Laocoon and the serpents
scenes.summary: Serpents kill Laocoon and his sons. The Trojans take it as punishment and drag the horse into the city despite Cassandra.
scenes.stakes: Troy's fate is sealed by admitting the horse.

scenes.title: Night: Hector's warning
scenes.summary: The Greeks leave the horse and open the gates. Hector's ghost warns Æneas to flee and entrusts him with the gods; Æneas wakes to the burning city.
scenes.stakes: Æneas's life and Troy's gods are at risk.

scenes.title: Street fighting
scenes.summary: Æneas joins Panthus and young warriors. They don Greek armour, but are betrayed by Trojan darts when Coroebus tries to rescue Cassandra, and most die.
scenes.stakes: Æneas and his companions face death.

scenes.title: The fall of Priam
scenes.summary: Pyrrhus breaks into the palace, kills Polites before his parents, and then kills Priam at the altar.
scenes.stakes: Priam and his family face slaughter.

scenes.title: Venus halts Æneas
scenes.summary: Æneas sees Helen and wants to kill her, but Venus stops him and reveals the gods destroying Troy, then guides him home.
scenes.stakes: Æneas risks death and neglects his family.

scenes.title: Anchises yields
scenes.summary: Anchises refuses to leave until the flame on Iulus's head and a falling star convince him. Æneas plans to carry him out.
scenes.stakes: The family faces death if Anchises will not leave.

scenes.title: Flight and loss of Creusa
scenes.summary: Creusa is lost on the way out. Æneas searches the city and meets her ghost, who foretells Hesperia, and he leads the exiles to the mountains.
scenes.stakes: Æneas loses his wife and risks his life in the city.

alias_notes.explanation: Pyrrhus is also called Neoptolemus, son of Achilles.
Æneas's son is called both Iulus and Ascanius.
Helen is identified by her father.
Patronymic of Achilles, son of Peleus.

notable_quotes.reason: Laocoon's famous warning, the source of 'beware of Greeks bearing gifts'.
Æneas's despairing maxim: the vanquished's only safety is to hope for none.
Narrator's comment on the folly of defying the gods.

analysis.text: Fate and divine will overwhelm human effort: Troy falls through gods and deceit, and Æneas must accept his destiny to found a new city.
Virgil gives Rome a Trojan origin, tying Augustan Rome to Homeric legend and casting Æneas's duty to family and gods as Roman pietas.

legacy.text: The phrase 'Trojan horse' and the saying 'beware of Greeks bearing gifts' derive from this book; the term also names malicious software.
The film Troy (2004) dramatises the horse and the sack of the city, though its story draws on several ancient sources.

fun_facts.text: Laocoon's death by serpents inspired the famous Hellenistic sculpture Laocoön and His Sons, rediscovered in Rome in 1506.

language_notes.text: Myrmidons were Achilles' followers and Dolopes another Greek contingent; Ulysses' band means his crew. Together they stand for all the Greek enemies.
Pallas is Minerva (Athena), the goddess of craft and war, who favored the Greeks and was said to have inspired the horse's design.
The Greeks give a vow for safe return as their pretext, the reason they offer publicly. 'Such the fame that spreads' means that was the story put about.
Mycenæ was the city of Agamemnon, the Greek commander, so it stands for Greece and the Greeks' home.
Dorian here simply means Greek; the Trojans use it for the enemy camp.
'Agaze' means gazing in wonder. The 'virgin goddess' is Pallas (Minerva), to whom the horse is offered.
'Had but... been unwarped' is a contrary-to-fact condition: if fate and human judgment had not been twisted, Troy would still stand.
Dardan means Trojan, from Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojan royal line. Achæans is another name for the Greeks.
Phrygian is used here as a synonym for Trojan; Danaans likewise means Greeks.
Palamedes was a Greek hero who, in later tradition, was framed by Ulysses for treachery and put to death. Sinon claims kinship with him.
The Ithacan is Ulysses, king of Ithaca. The sons of Atreus are Agamemnon and Menelaus, the Greek leaders.
The maiden's slaughter refers to Iphigenia, sacrificed by Agamemnon to win winds for the Greek fleet sailing to Troy.
Salt cakes and fillet: sacrificial meal sprinkled on the victim and the woollen headband it wore.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes. He and Ulysses stole the Palladium, the sacred statue of Pallas that protected Troy.
Achilles of Larissa: Achilles is linked to Thessaly, where Larissa lies. Pelasgians and Danaans are other names for the Greeks.
"Drawn by lot" means Laocoon was chosen by lottery to serve as Neptune's priest for this occasion.
"Manes" here means crests; the serpents' raised, blood-red crests are likened to a mane. "Main" means the open sea.
"Spires" means coils coiled like a spiral, here the serpents' winding bodies.
"Fillets" are the ribbons or headbands a priest wore; "gore" is clotted blood.
Tritonia is a title of Minerva (the Greek Athena), whose statue stands in the citadel temple; the serpents take refuge at her feet.
Laocoon's "crime" refers to his hurling a spear at the horse, which the Trojans now see as sacrilege against Minerva's offering.
"Engine" means a machine or contrivance; the horse is called a fateful engine because it is a war device carrying armed men.
Ilion is Troy; "home of the gods" recalls that gods such as Neptune and Apollo were said to have built its walls.
"Dardan" means Trojan, from Dardanus, legendary ancestor of the Trojan royal line.
Cassandra was a Trojan princess given prophecy by Apollo, who then doomed her never to be believed.
Myrmidon wiles: the Myrmidons were Achilles' people; here the name stands for the Greeks generally, and their tricks (the wooden horse) are hidden by night.
Danaans and Argives are both names for the Greeks; Tenedos is the island where their fleet had hidden.
"that treacherous womb" means the hollow belly of the wooden horse, which hid the armed men.
Hector was killed by Achilles, who dragged his body behind a chariot, his feet pierced by thongs.
Hector had worn the armour of Achilles, taken from Patroclus whom he killed, and had hurled fire at the Greek ships.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy; "goddess-born" addresses Æneas, son of Venus.
Vesta was goddess of the hearth; her fillets (sacred headbands) and eternal fire are Troy's sacred emblems, which Hector entrusts to Æneas.
"Fire-god" is Vulcan, used for fire itself; Sigean refers to Sigeum, the headland near Troy.
Achæan means Greek; Phœbus is Apollo. Panthus is his priest in the citadel (Pergamus).
"Sons of Teucer" means the Trojans, named after Teucer, an early king of Troy; Dardan likewise means Trojan.
Sinon is the Greek who pretended to be a deserter and persuaded the Trojans to take the wooden horse inside.
Cassandra was a prophetess cursed by Apollo never to be believed; she warned of Troy's fall, so she is "heaven-struck".
"Queened it" uses a noun as a verb: the city ruled like a queen.
Cassandra had taken refuge at Minerva's statue; Ajax (son of Oileus) dragged her away, an act of sacrilege.
Dolopes were a Thessalian people who fought under Pyrrhus (Achilles' son). Nereus here stands for the sea.
"Fillet" is a priestly headband, a sign of Apollo's service that offered no protection.
Danaans is Virgil's name for the Greeks; the 'penthouse of shields' is a testudo-like roof of interlocked shields protecting men at the door.
Postern means a back or side door, here a hidden private passage in the palace.
Pyrrhus, also called Neoptolemus, is Achilles' son, brought from Scyros to fight at Troy after his father's death.
Valves means the leaves or panels of a double door.
The Atridæ are Agamemnon and Menelaus, sons of Atreus, leaders of the Greek expedition.
Priam says Pyrrhus's 'lying tongue' calls Achilles his sire: he denies Pyrrhus is worthy of his father, who once respected Priam's plea for Hector's body.
Pelides, 'son of Peleus,' is a name for Achilles.
The nameless corpse on the shore is often read as an allusion to Pompey's death, though this is debated.
Creusa is Æneas's wife, a daughter of Priam; Iulus is another name for his son Ascanius, named in sentence 218.
The daughter of Tyndareus is Helen, called after her mortal father; she caused the war by going to Troy with Paris.
Teucrians are the Trojans, and Danaans are the Greeks; Pergamus is the citadel of Troy.
Phrygian means Trojan; Phrygia is the region of Asia Minor in which Troy lay.
Dardan means Trojan, after Dardanus, the founder of the Trojan line.
"Slaked the thirsty ashes" means satisfying the spirits of the dead Trojans, who were thought to crave vengeance.
Neptune built Troy's walls with Apollo for Laomedon, so here he tears down his own work. The Scæan gate was Troy's main gate.
Tritonian Pallas is Minerva (Athena); the Gorgon's head is on her aegis (shield-cloak).
The great Father is Jove (Jupiter), king of the gods, who now supports the Greeks.
The 'one sack' is the earlier capture of Troy by Hercules in Laomedon's reign, which Anchises lived through.
Going unburied was dreaded in the ancient world, since proper burial was needed for the dead's rest. Anchises dismisses it.
Anchises was said to have been struck by Jove's lightning for boasting of Venus's love, leaving him lame or crippled.
Pyrrhus, also called Neoptolemus, is Achilles' son. He has just killed Priam at the altar, after killing Priam's son Polites before him.
'Gracious mother' addresses Venus, Æneas's divine mother, who had earlier led him from the burning city.
Danaans is a name for the Greeks, from Danaus, a legendary king of Argos.
'Innocuous' means harmless: the flame plays about the boy's hair without burning it.
Thunder 'on the left' was a favourable omen in Roman augury, so Anchises reads it as Jove's assent.
A cypress was associated with death and mourning, so the old tree suits a meeting place outside a ruined city.
The lion's skin is laid over his shoulders as a cover so Anchises can be carried on his back.
"Erewhile" is archaic for "a short time before"; "quailed" means shrank in fear.
Ceres is the Roman goddess of grain; her old mound and temple was the agreed gathering point outside the city.
"Teucrian" means Trojan, from Teucer, an early king of the Trojan land. The household gods are the Penates, carried from Troy.
Phœnix here is a Greek guard, not the Phœnix of the Iliad; the Greeks are guarding plunder in Juno's temple.
Hesperia means "western land," i.e. Italy. "Lydia's river" refers to the tradition that the Etruscans, who lived by the Tiber, came from Lydia.
"Heaven's mighty mother" is Cybele, the Great Mother goddess; Creusa stays under her protection. Venus is Æneas's mother, hence "daughter by marriage."
Three failed embraces of a ghost echo Ulysses's meeting with his mother in the Odyssey, a classic epic scene.

context_notes.text: Tenedos is a small island near the Trojan coast, where the Greek fleet hid to feign departure.
Thymœtes is a Trojan who urges bringing the horse in; Virgil leaves his motive uncertain.
Laocoon is a priest of Neptune, who warns his countrymen against the horse.
Phœbus is Apollo, whose oracles, notably at Delphi, were consulted on important decisions.
Priam is the aged king of Troy. His pity here helps seal the city's fate.
Tritonia is a title of Pallas Athena (Minerva), the Greek goddess of war and wisdom, who favoured the Greeks.
Tenedos is an island near Troy where the Greek fleet is secretly hiding, pretending to have sailed away.
The Trojans think dedicating the horse to Minerva will win her favour, not knowing Greek soldiers are hidden inside.
Sinon is the Greek who had let himself be captured and persuaded the Trojans to take the horse inside the city.
The named Greek leaders include Ulysses, Neoptolemus (Achilles' son), Menelaus, and Epeus, who built the horse.
Deiphobus and Ucalegon are Trojan nobles whose houses burn first.
Androgeos was a Greek leader; here he mistakes the disguised-free Trojans for Greek reinforcements in the dark.
The "womb" is the wooden horse in which the Greeks had hidden.
Andromache was Hector's wife; Astyanax was their young son, later killed by the Greeks.
Hecuba was Priam's queen. Priam had fifty sons, so many daughters-in-law lived in the palace.
Household altars with a sacred tree stood in the open courtyard; the bay (laurel) was sacred to Apollo.
Æneas has just watched Pyrrhus kill old King Priam, which reminds him of his own father Anchises.
Venus is Æneas's mother, and she appears in her true divine form, not disguised.
Juno was Troy's bitter enemy throughout the Æneid, favouring the Greeks and later opposing Æneas.
Ascanius is another name for Iulus, Æneas's young son. Creusa is Æneas's wife, who will be lost in the flight.
Ceres was the goddess of grain and harvest. Her lonely temple outside Troy is the agreed rendezvous.
Roman custom required ritual purity before handling sacred objects, and contact with blood or killing defiled a person.
Iulus is Æneas's young son, also called Ascanius; Roman tradition made him ancestor of the Julian family, including Augustus.
Myrmidons and Dolopes were Greek peoples under Achilles and Pyrrhus. Creusa says she will escape being a captive slave.
Ida is the mountain near Troy. Dawn arrives as the exiles realise that Troy is lost for good.

literary_notes.text: Æneas speaks as first-person survivor and eyewitness, opening with reluctance; this lends the tale authority and pathos.
Night 'rushing' down the sky and the stars 'counseling' rest give the evening a human, urging presence.
Troy 'shakes off' the agony of years as if it were a burden or sickness, underlining false relief.
The horse is called a 'hollow womb', an image that sets up its secret and deadly brood of warriors.
The narrator's remark that Troy might still stand shows the missed chance and anticipates the city's fall.
Aeneas, narrating to Dido, steps outside the story to address her directly and gives his own judgment of the Greeks.
Sinon's cry presents him as helpless and hunted, a performance that wins sympathy.
Sinon's tone of sincerity is called false, so the reader sees the lie behind the pity.
Calling the horse a mountain stresses its enormous size and the awe it inspires.
Aeneas, narrating with hindsight, knows that the Trojans' belief in Sinon's tale brought about their ruin.
"Unprophetic souls" hints that the Trojans cannot foresee the disaster this portent leads to.
Vivid colour, motion and sound, such as blood-red crests, foaming brine and hissing tongues, make the serpents terrifying.
Laocoon's cries are compared to a wounded bull escaping the altar, echoing the sacrifice he was performing.
The narrator breaks off to address his lost city directly, expressing grief.
The horse stopping four times and the clash of hidden arms warn of doom, but the Trojans ignore them.
The reader knows Cassandra's warnings are true while the Trojans celebrate on their last day.
Night is pictured as coming from the ocean and wrapping the world in shade, setting an ominous mood before the attack.
The triumphant Hector of the past is set against the mangled ghost, making the fall of Troy felt.
Æneas's alarm is compared to a shepherd hearing a distant wildfire or flood, conveying helpless, bewildered dread.
Æneas's frenzied rush to arms shows his heroic, impulsive courage and his desire for a glorious death.
Hope lies in giving up hope; the maxim sums up the Trojans' doomed courage.
The Trojans are compared to starving wolves hunting at night, conveying desperation and savagery, with cubs waiting at home to heighten pathos.
Androgeos recoiling is likened to a man who steps on a snake, turning the Greek into the startled victim.
The narrator's sudden moral exclamation interrupts the story, warning that fighting against divine will is futile.
The Greek counterattack is compared to clashing winds and a storm-tossed sea, magnifying its force.
Pyrrhus is compared to a renewed serpent, suggesting menace, youthful vigor and a deadly, glittering rebirth.
The flood breaking its banks conveys the irresistible, destructive rush of the Greeks into the palace.
The narrator's exclamation 'poor old man!' shows Aeneas's pity for Priam.
Frightened doves in a storm convey the helpless huddling of Hecuba and her daughters.
Priam is killed at the altar in his son's blood, an ironic reversal of the sanctuary he sought.
The repeated "There rose up" in this and the next sentence shows how his thoughts of family flood in.
Æneas's angry questions show how he justifies murder to himself and build up his rage.
Venus tells him that the gods, not Helen or Paris, are to blame, which changes how Æneas understands the war.
Venus vanishes into thick darkness, which is a contrast with her earlier radiance.
The falling of Troy is compared to a mountain ash felled by woodmen, which shows the slow collapse of a great city.
Anchises calls himself a 'clog on time' and says Jove laid 'the finger of flame' on him, describing his life as dead weight and his lightning-strike as a divine touch.
A run of questions expresses Æneas's shock and shows how strongly he rejects the idea of abandoning his father.
The repeated 'who butchers' piles up Pyrrhus's crimes and makes the threat feel immediate and brutal.
The harmless flame on Iulus's head is an omen of the boy's future greatness and of divine protection for the family.
The falling star's torchlike train, the furrowed line of light and the sulphurous smoke make the omen vivid and sensory.
Æneas's offer to carry his father shows the dutiful devotion (pietas) that defines him in the poem.
The warrior who was fearless in battle is now terrified by every sound, showing how fear for his family unmans him.
Destiny is pictured as a force that physically "tore" Creusa away, presenting her loss as beyond his control.
The fire is described as triumphant and streaming madly, as if it were a conquering army.
The ghost's unnaturally large size and sudden appearance create an eerie supernatural moment.
The phantom is compared to wind and to the wings of sleep, stressing that she cannot be touched.
